claim: Formal Proposition (Gradient Conflict): for an over-confident model where Conf_theta(x) > E_y~pi_theta[R(y)], the Fisher-metric inner product between the accuracy-maximizing gradient and the calibration-error-minimizing gradient equals -(dl/dc)*Cov_pi_theta(R(y),phi(y)), which is strictly negative whenever accuracy and the confidence feature are positively correlated (Cov>0) -- i.e. the two gradients are provably anti-aligned under naive joint/coupled optimization.
stance_target: a single joint scalar objective/reward that sums or otherwise couples an accuracy term and a calibration-error term can be optimized without an inherent, provable gradient conflict
scope_conditions: any coupled RLVR objective of the form J_acc(theta) + calibration-loss coupling, when the model is over-confident and Cov_pi(R,phi)>0
quoted_support: Proposition 4.2 (Gradient Conflict). If the model is over-confident: Conf_theta(x) > E_y~pi_theta[R(y)], then the ascent direction of J_acc and J_cal satisfy <grad_theta J_acc(theta), grad_theta J_cal(theta)>_{F^-1} < 0.

claim: Formal Proposition (Mode Collapse): in the absence of explicit entropy regularization, the optimal solution to unregularized trajectory-level accuracy maximization max_theta J_acc(theta) is a linear program over the response probability simplex whose optimum places probability mass 1 on a single correct trajectory y*.
stance_target: trajectory-level RLVR training has a structural, provable tendency toward degenerate collapse of the output distribution (and by extension confidence distribution) even before any calibration term is added
scope_conditions: trajectory-level RLVR with binary correctness reward, no entropy regularization
quoted_support: Proposition 4.1 (Mode Collapse). In the absence of explicit entropy regularization, any optimal solution to max_theta J_acc(theta) assigns probability mass 1 to a single trajectory y* in Y+.

claim: DCPO's objective genuinely decouples reasoning and confidence at the token level: output is split into a reasoning block o_r and a verbalized confidence block o_c via a <conf> delimiter; separate GRPO-style group-relative advantages A_r (binary correctness reward) and A_c (an absolute-error/proper-scoring confidence reward against a hybrid instance+group-level accuracy target) are applied only to their own token subsets via a masked gradient.
stance_target: structurally decoupling accuracy and calibration gradients at the token/advantage level (rather than fusing them into one scalar reward) mechanically avoids the proven gradient conflict
quoted_support: we prompt the model to generate a response o in the following structured form o=[o_r <conf> o_c]... advantages signals are applied exclusively to their corresponding token subsets.

claim: The confidence reward is R_c(o_c) = -|confidence(o_c) - R_IG|, where R_IG = lambda*R_tilde_G + (1-lambda)*R(o_r) is a hybrid target interpolating group-level accuracy R_tilde_G (mean correctness over the G rollouts in a group) and instance-level correctness R(o_r); group-level accuracy is proven to be an unbiased, variance-O(1/G) estimator of true correctness probability, providing lower-variance calibration supervision than raw per-instance binary labels.
stance_target: instance-level binary correctness alone is an insufficiently stable supervision signal for calibration training; a group-averaged accuracy target reduces gradient variance
scope_conditions: GRPO-style group rollout sampling, group size G
quoted_support: Proposition 4.3. tilde{R}_G is an unbiased estimator of E[R(y)] with variance O(1/G)... Proposition 4.4... using tilde{R}_G as supervision reduces gradient variance compared to instance-level correctness.

claim: DCPO reports discrimination (AUROC) alongside calibration (ECE, PCE) and accuracy separately for every method and benchmark, e.g. on AIME25: DCPO Acc=28.3/ECE=0.130/PCE=0.133/AUROC=0.951 vs GRPO Acc=29.2/ECE=0.469/PCE=0.556/AUROC=0.742 vs RLCR Acc=24.1/ECE=0.134/PCE=0.138/AUROC=0.621 -- RLCR trades off ~5 points of accuracy for calibration while also underperforming DCPO on AUROC.
stance_target: decoupled objectives (DCPO) achieve better joint accuracy+discrimination+calibration than either uncoupled RLVR (GRPO) or coupled joint-reward baselines (RLCR, CCGSPG)
numbers: DCPO AIME25: Acc 28.3, ECE 0.130, PCE 0.133, AUROC 0.951
GRPO AIME25: Acc 29.2, ECE 0.469, PCE 0.556, AUROC 0.742
RLCR AIME25: Acc 24.1, ECE 0.134, PCE 0.138, AUROC 0.621
overall DCPO ECE reduced from 0.435 (base) to 0.128, a 71.6% relative reduction

claim: GRPO training on Qwen3-8B raises average predicted confidence from about 0.88 to above 0.98 while shrinking confidence variance from 0.006 to about 0.001, and raises Positive Calibration Error (PCE, ECE restricted to over-confident bins) from 0.312 to 0.362 -- direct empirical evidence of confidence-distribution narrowing/collapse toward a single high value during RLVR training.
stance_target: RLVR training causes the confidence distribution to collapse toward a narrow, near-1.0 range even as reasoning accuracy improves
scope_conditions: Qwen3-8B (non-thinking), GRPO training on DeepScaler dataset, evaluated on AIME24 with 8 repeated samplings
quoted_support: GRPO steadily increases the model's average confidence from about 0.88 to above 0.98, and decrease model confidence variance from 0.006 to about 0.001... after GRPO training, PCE increases from 0.312 to 0.362.

claim: Comparing standard GRPO against two coupled calibration-aware methods (RLCR, CCGSPG) on AIME24 shows both coupled methods substantially reduce ECE/PCE relative to GRPO but at the cost of a noticeable reasoning-accuracy drop, empirically confirming the accuracy-calibration tradeoff predicted by the gradient-conflict theorem.
stance_target: empirically-observed accuracy-calibration tradeoffs in prior coupled-objective methods (RLCR, CCGSPG) are a direct consequence of the proven gradient conflict, not an implementation artifact
scope_conditions: Qwen3-8B, AIME24 benchmark, comparing GRPO vs RLCR vs CCGSPG
quoted_support: both RLCR and CCGSPG substantially reduce ECE and PCE compared to GRPO, indicating improved calibration, while both methods exhibit a noticeable reasoning accuracy performance drop relative to GRPO.

claim: DCPO experiments were run with Qwen3-8B via full-parameter RL fine-tuning (VERL framework) on 8x NVIDIA A100 80GB GPUs, batch size 256 (math) or 128 (code), group rollout size 8, 3 epochs (~120 steps for math) -- a substantial multi-GPU compute budget with no LoRA/PEFT variant reported.
stance_target: single-GPU 7-8B-scale feasibility of decoupled calibration-aware RL training
quoted_support: All reinforcement learning experiments are conducted using the VERL framework on a cluster of 8 NVIDIA A100 (80GB) GPUs.
